passage: Nitin spent Monday and Tuesday building his own way of grouping delivery routes in the Hyderabad office. He was proud of one idea: storing locations in a grid, so nearby points sit next to each other in memory. On Wednesday morning he did what he had skipped at the start and read how the standard routing library works. Hafsa, who had used it for years, walked him through its parts. The library handled cases he hadn't reached: one-way streets, closed roads, ties. But its data layout was slower for his long lists. He kept his grid for loading the data and used the library for the routing. The result ran faster than either alone. 'Two days well spent,' said Hafsa. 'Two days and a bit of humility,' said Nitin.

"Two days," Tejas said, looking at the whiteboard covered in Deepak's diagrams. "You've been building your own caching method for two days."
"I know." Deepak rubbed his eyes. "And I think part of it is actually good. But I've been stuck on expiry for six hours."
"Have you looked at how the standard library does it?"
"I didn't want to. I wanted to see if I could reason it out."
"You did reason it out. Now compare."
Deepak opened the library's documentation beside his notes. For twenty minutes he read quietly. Then he laughed.
"Their expiry handling is far better than mine. Timers, edge cases, all of it. But look, my way of laying out the data in memory is simpler than theirs, and faster for our use."
"So?"
"So I keep my data layout and use their library for everything else." He erased half the whiteboard. "Should've looked yesterday."

I'm Pranav. Last month I spent two days building my own way to sort our warehouse orders. I was proud of it. I'd worked it out on paper from scratch.
Then my manager Farhan asked a simple question in the corridor: "Have you compared it with the standard sorting routines?"
I hadn't. Honestly, I was scared they'd be better and my two days would look silly.
That evening I made myself do it. I ran my method and the standard one on the same ten thousand orders. The standard one was faster on almost everything, and it handled weird cases like two orders with the same timestamp.
But mine did one thing better. I'd grouped orders by loading bay before sorting, and that cut the sorting work in half for our warehouse.
So I kept my grouping step and used the standard routine for the sorting itself. Farhan looked at the numbers and just said, "Good. Both."
